title: Parliament pays tribute to music icon Nanda Malini | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 22 August 2026 00:39
-     - 2

House observes minute’s silence on proposal by PM

 Celebrated singer passes away aged 82

 PM hails contribution to music, culture and social discourse

 Opposition Leader remembers artist who stood by her principles

Nanda Malini

Parliament yesterday observed a minute’s silence in memory of veteran singer Dr. Nanda Malini, who passed away aged 82, following a proposal by Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya.

Delivering a condolence message on behalf of the Government, the Prime Minister said Malini’s passing marked the loss of an artist whose voice had accompanied generations of Sri Lankans through nearly seven decades.

She recalled Malini’s entry into cinema music through ‘Ran Muthu Doova’ under the mentorship of Dr. W.D. Amaradeva and said her work extended beyond music to reflect the struggles, hopes and experiences of society.

Dr. Amarasuriya said Malini used her art to speak against injustice and for peace, coexistence, humanity and social justice, citing works including ‘Pavana’ and ‘Sathyaye Geethaya’.

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa also paid tribute, describing Malini as a “democratic artist” who remained committed to her principles and stood for fundamental rights and humanitarian values during difficult periods in the country’s history.

Born on 23 August 1943, Malini became one of Sri Lanka’s most recognised voices during a career spanning nearly seven decades.

Her remains will lie at her residence on Wijayaba Mawatha, Nawala, for the public to pay their respects. Religious rites will be held at 3:30 p.m. tomorrow, followed by cremation at the Borella Cemetery at 5 p.m. In accordance with her final wishes, there will be no formal funeral ceremony.

title: Govt. steps up preparations for El Niño threat: President’s Office | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 22 August 2026 00:37
-     - 2

The Government has stepped up preparations to mitigate the economic and livelihood impact of expected El Niño-driven dry weather, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake yesterday reviewing plans covering agriculture, water supply, electricity generation, plantation industries and food security.

According to the President’s Media Division, the review came at a meeting of the Special Cabinet Sub-Committee and Officials’ Committee on El Niño at the Presidential Secretariat, after the Department of Meteorology forecast severe dry weather across the country during February, March and April 2027.

President Dissanayake instructed officials to ensure uninterrupted essential goods and services and prepare support programs for affected communities in coordination with disaster management authorities.

The Government is also preparing water-management measures ahead of the dry period, including identifying vulnerable areas and planning any necessary water restrictions before reservoirs reach critical levels.

Preparations for the upcoming Maha season include ensuring seed paddy and fertiliser availability and using expected October rainfall to prepare agricultural land rather than waiting for reservoir releases. The President also called for irrigation rehabilitation to be expedited to maximise water storage from the expected rains.

On energy, officials discussed maintaining a planned reserve of electricity generation capacity above normal requirements to protect power supplies against risks from depleted reservoirs during February-April 2027.

The President also directed officials to prepare measures for potential impacts on plantation industries and freshwater fisheries, including livelihood support for affected fishing communities.

title: National Youth Innovation Challenge to mark World Food Day in Sri Lanka
Before sirens, Sri Lanka puts its young people on front line | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 22 August 2026 00:28
-     - 0

By Tania de Silva

The real test of a disaster warning is not whether it is issued. It is whether somebody, somewhere, hears it in time.

In a village threatened by a rising river, somebody may be a young person knocking on a neighbour’s door. It may be the volunteer who knows where an elderly man lives alone, or the youth leader who remembers that a pregnant woman in the community cannot simply be swept into the nearest evacuation centre.

It was with this less glamourous, but considerably more important, business of preparedness that more than 100 young Sri Lankans gathered in Maharagama on Wednesday, 12 August 2026.

The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), in partnership with the National Youth Services Council (NYSC) and under Youth Affairs and Sports Ministry brought youth leaders from across the country together for a national simulation exercise titled The Resilience Lab: Local Youth Action in Crisis Response.

The exercise, held to mark International Youth Day, was built around this year’s theme, “Different Contexts, Shared Aspirations.”

But there was little ceremony about the day.

The young participants were placed in simulated emergencies, floods, landslides and a dengue outbreak, and asked to make decisions that, in a real crisis, could carry consequences far beyond a classroom.

The purpose was straightforward: to move Sri Lanka’s disaster thinking a step backwards, from the ambulance at the scene to the warning before the siren; from relief after the catastrophe to preparation before it.

The need is difficult to dispute.

The devastation caused by Cyclone Ditwah remains a stark reference point. Some 2.2 million people were affected, more than 600 lives were lost and nearly 115,000 homes were damaged.

For disaster agencies, such figures become statistics. For families, they become empty chairs at dinner tables, damaged houses and months spent putting ordinary life back together.

It is precisely here that Sri Lanka’s youth network could become an unlikely national asset.

The 2024 Census places the number of people aged between 15 and 29 at approximately 4.78 million , nearly 22 per cent of the population.

And through the NYSC, the Government has an existing network of around 14,000 Youth Clubs, reaching more than 280,000 young people at community level.

The question, then, is not whether the country has young people.

It is whether it has prepared them.

NYSC Chairman and Youth Affairs Director General, Attorney-at-Law Supun Wijerathna, said the experience of Cyclone Ditwah had demonstrated how quickly the organisation’s network could be called upon when disaster struck.

The young, he said, possessed something emergency systems could not manufacture overnight — time, flexibility, energy and a connection with their communities.

But the ambition is larger than producing volunteers who arrive after the damage is done.

“We need to have a clear vision of what we are trying to build,” Wijerathna said.

The vision, he explained, was of young leaders who could disseminate warnings, organise communities and act before disaster became disaster.

That distinction may prove crucial.

An early warning which does not reach the elderly woman living alone is not much of a warning. A flood evacuation plan which ignores a person with a disability is not much of a plan. And an emergency response which overlooks the healthcare needs of a pregnant woman has, at its heart, already failed.

That was why the simulations placed particular emphasis on reaching what officials described as “the last person”.

The phrase sounds administrative. Its meaning is not.

It is the difference between a warning being broadcast and a warning being understood. Between a government instruction and a neighbour taking responsibility for a neighbour.

UNFPA Sri Lanka Assistant Representative Dr. Dayanath Ranatunga, said young people should not be regarded merely as passive beneficiaries of disaster relief.

“They are active communicators, first responders, and community mobilisers,” he said.

The program also brought sexual and reproductive health and rights, together with gender considerations, into the emergency scenarios, areas that can be pushed to the margins when the immediate concerns are water, shelter and food.

Yet emergencies do not suspend ordinary human needs.

They often make them more urgent.

The Resilience Lab was organised with technical support from the Disaster Management Centre, the Sri Lanka Red Cross Society and the Family Planning Association of Sri Lanka.

Its significance, however, will not be measured by what happened inside the NYSC auditorium.

It will be measured later, perhaps on a wet night when a river begins to rise, when a landslide warning comes through a mobile phone, or when an outbreak begins in a neighbourhood already struggling with inadequate services.

Then there will be no podium, no microphones and no carefully prepared program.

There will simply be a warning, and a short space of time in which somebody must decide what to do with it.

Sri Lanka has spent years learning how to respond to disasters.

The more difficult lesson is learning how to prevent them from becoming tragedies.

And that lesson, increasingly, is being placed in the hands of the young.

title: EU, Sri Lanka discuss stronger economic ties as Ambassador departs | Daily FT

Sri Lanka and the European Union (EU) discussed further strengthening bilateral cooperation and economic relations during a meeting between European Union Ambassador to Sri Lanka and the Maldives Carmen Moreno and Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando.

title: Korea announces opening of Visa Application Centre; changes to Visa procedures | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 22 August 2026 00:19
-     - 1

Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Sri Lanka said yesterday it will introduce changes to its visa application procedures in connection with the opening of the Visa Application Centre on 21 August 2026.

Following the opening of the Visa Application Centre, visa applications, as well as the submission and collection of passports in connection with visa applications, will only be handled through the Visa Application Centre.

Applicants will be required to submit their visa applications and passports through the Visa Application Centre, and passports with issued visas will be returned to applicants through the Visa Application Centre. All the visa applicants are required to make a prior appointment through the Visa Application Centre’s website: https://visaforkorea-sl.com/

The Embassy will continue to accept Diplomatic and Official visa applications accompanied by a Third Person Note (TPN) issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism of Sri Lanka directly at the Embassy.

Official Name: VFS Global Visa Application Centre in Colombo, No. 675, Dr. Danister De Silva Mawatha, Colombo 09, Sri Lanka. Contact Number: +94-11-235-0629; Email: info.koreasl@vfshelpline.com

Following the opening of the Visa Application Centre, the Embassy’s current online reservation procedure for visa applications will no longer be available.

However, the Embassy will continue to handle applications for notarisation services and Police Clearance Certificates (Criminal Records Certificates) directly, as is currently the case. Accordingly, the Embassy’s online reservation system for these services will remain.

The Embassy said it appreciates the public’s understanding and cooperation regarding these changes and expects that the new system will contribute to a more efficient and convenient visa application process.
